name: Biatah Bidayuh
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress; 1 further work by the same author (or citing it for stress) agrees.
sweep_summary: Both works with stress in the title are the same work: Rensch's 'Rhythm in Bidayuh' as a 2006 10-ICAL web paper (the catalog's current deciding source, already held by the project) and as its 2008 print version in Studies in Philippine Languages and Cultures 19: 84-91, which I located via the archived SIL Philippines SPLC 19 contents/download pages and downloaded from an Internet Archive copy (live SIL URL is 404). The published version repeats the stress statement verbatim (p. 85: 'Stress falls on the ultima of the Bidayuh word, at least in isolation'), adds nothing dialect-specific for Biatah, and confirms the fixed-dominant (final) coding; its penult full/reduced contrast is explained as a reflex of PAN final vs penultimate accent, a historical claim, not a synchronic stress alternation. The 2008 citation should be preferred over the 2006 web paper as the citable form of the same source, but it does not supersede it in content. Nothing new to acquire from this search of works with stress in the title; our earlier reading's list of works to obtain (Sulissusiawan et al. 1999 Fonologi bahasa Bedayuh; Kroeger 1996; Darmansyah et al. 1994) stands.

new_statements.quote: Bidayuh stems are typically disyllabic. Stress falls on the ultima of the Bidayuh word, at least in isolation.
new_statements.citation: Rensch, Calvin R. 2008. Rhythm in Bidayuh. Studies in Philippine Languages and Cultures 19: 84-91. SIL Philippines.
new_statements.reading: Fixed word-final (ultima) stress across Bidayuh, stated by the principal Bidayuh specialist for all four dialect clusters with Biatah as the Central exemplar; hedged to citation/isolation forms. Consistent with the catalog's fixed-dominant coding and with Rensch et al. 2012 (SIL e-Book 33, p. 47: ultima 'receives the peak of word stress—at least in citation forms'). The 2008 text is word-for-word the 2006 conference statement.
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File opened: (8 pp, text; header reads 'Studies in Philippine Languages and Cultures Volume 19 (2008), 84-91'). Quote confirmed verbatim at p. 2 = printed p. 85, first paragraph of sec. 2 'Rhythm differences' (extracted the text): 'Bidayuh stems are typically disyllabic. Stress falls on the ultima of the Bidayuh [line break] word, at least in isolation.' The 2006 10-ICAL conference PDF (same folder, lines 59-60) carries the identical sentence, so the 2008 article is the published version of the same paper, not a new statement. Surrounding passage: the rest of sec. 2 (pp. 85-88) is about vowel duration (ultima normal vs lengthened; penult full vs reduced) framed as 'rhythm', not stress place…

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation from Rensch 2006 is verbatim at sec. 2, p.2 of the file downloaded now from the SIL 10-ICAL mirror named in the citation. (2) Deciding source is a 2006 specialist phonology conference paper covering all Bidayuh clusters with Biatah as the Central exemplar; the fuller source, Rensch et al. 2012 (SIL e-Book 33, 517 pp; Part II is a cross-dialect Bidayuh phonology that treats Biatah throughout), was already held by the project under buka1257 and is now copied into the biat1246 folder. It independently states final (ultima) word stress in citation forms (p.47), adds that enclitics take the stress (fn.79 p.94) and that Land Dayak languages 'consistently accent the final syllable of the stem; especially evident in utterance-final position' (p.292). Nothing found contradicts

sources.quote: Bidayuh stems are typically disyllabic. Stress falls on the ultima of the Bidayuh word, at least in isolation.

sources.citation: Rensch, Calvin R. 2008. Rhythm in Bidayuh. Studies in Philippine Languages and Cultures 19 (10-ICAL Borneo, Sulawesi & Philippines Papers, ed. Phil Quick & Joanna Smith, SIL Philippines): 84-91.
sources.quote: Bidayuh stems are typically disyllabic. Stress falls on the ultima of the Bidayuh word, at least in isolation. [p. 85] ... In Western Bidayuh vowels may be rearticulated, i.e., there are sequences of identical (or diverse) vowels with the onset of the second vowel marked by an articulatory pulse coinciding with the onset of stress. [fn. 3, p. 86] ... a Bidayuh form with a full vowel has developed from an earlier form with final stress while a Bidayuh form with a reduced vowel has developed from an earlier form with penultimate stress. [p. 90]
sources.locator: sec. 2 'Rhythm differences', p. 85 (p. 2); fn. 3 p. 86; sec. 3.2 p. 90
sources.note: Published (peer-edited) version of the 2006 conference paper, same text: pan-Bidayuh (25 dialects, four clusters; Biatah is the Central-cluster exemplar dialect cited in secs. 2.1-2.2) word stress on the ultima, hedged 'at least in isolation'. The paper is mainly about vowel-duration rhythm (lengthened ultima vowels; full vs reduced penult vowels), which it derives historically from lost medial consonants and from PAN final vs penultimate accent; that is diachronic, not a synchronic alternative stress placement. No dialect-specific deviation from final stress is reported.

sources.citation: Rensch, Calvin R., Carolyn M. Rensch, Jonas Noeb & Robert Sulis Ridu. 2012. The Bidayuh Language: Yesterday, Today and Tomorrow. Revised and expanded. SIL e-Books 33. Dallas: SIL International. 517 pp. (local copy taken from; sil.org could not be reached by automated download)
sources.quote: p.47: "In Bidayuh the ultima (last syllable) is the nucleus of the word. It receives the peak of word stress—at least in citation forms (words that are pronounced individually)." p.94 fn.79: "Because word stress falls on the final syllable in Bidayuh citation forms, and perhaps in context, a clitic receives the stress placement in the word to which it is attached." p.292: "They consistently accent the final syllable of the stem; this is especially evident in utterance-final position." Biatah is one of the dialects covered throughout (c. 1000 mentions).
sources.locator: Part II (C. M. Rensch, Nasality in Bidayuh Phonology) sec. 4.1.2 p.47 (p.64); fn. 79 p.94 (p.111); Part III (C. R. Rensch, Studies of the early Bidayuh language) sec. 6.2.4 p.292 (p.309)

tone.quote: In Bidayuh the ultima (last syllable) is the nucleus of the word. It receives the peak of word stress—at least in citation forms (words that are pronounced individually). [...] When this kind of word is articulated carefully, a syllable juncture is audible between the two adjacent same vowels, as is a slight decay from the first vowel, which is the nucleus (or peak) of the penult, followed by a step-up of intensity and pitch on the second vowel, which is the nucleus (or peak) of the ultima.
